summary: Defines parameters and a PPP LCP extension for a standard way of using PPP to compress serial data in Data Circuit-Terminating Equipment, such as modems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets the modem box itself shrink data in a way that is agreed upon with the other side.

subtitle: Compression for modems and data equipment using PPP.

tldr.problem: Modems and other data equipment need a standard way to compress serial data using PPP, but different devices have different capabilities for negotiating compression parameters.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three operational modes: Mode-0 (transparent, no compression), Mode-1 (fixed compression with no negotiation), and Mode-2 (full PPP negotiation). It specifies a DCE-Identifier LCP extension and mandates the LZS-DCP compression algorithm for interoperability.
tldr.outcome: Modems can now compress traffic using a standardized set of parameters. Mode-1 provides simple operation for basic equipment, while Mode-2 offers flexibility for advanced devices.

today: RFC 1976 is Informational. It defines a specific application of PPP compression for DCE devices, particularly modems. Although written for synchronous serial equipment of the 1990s, the three-mode approach demonstrates how protocols can support both simple and advanced implementations for backward compatibility.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines how PPP can provide data compression in Data Circuit-Terminating Equipment (DCE) such as modems and DSU/CSU devices. It was developed by the TR30.1 ad hoc committee on compression of synchronous data to allow serial data compression in these network edge devices.

PPP provides three components: a method for encapsulating multi-protocol datagrams, a Link Control Protocol for setting up the connection, and Network Control Protocols for configuring different network layers. The RFC uses PPP's negotiation mechanism together with the PPP Compression Control Protocol to define a standard for DCE compression.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is a standard way to send data over point-to-point links. This RFC says how PPP can compress data in modems and similar boxes at the edge of the network.

sections.title: Three Modes of Operation
sections.content:
The RFC defines three operating modes to accommodate devices with different capabilities:

Mode-0 is transparent operation, representing currently deployed DCE devices that operate without any DCE-to-DCE protocols. Mode-1 implements fixed compression with no negotiation: when a Mode-1 device powers up, it uses a predetermined set of parameters and protocol packets. Mode-1 devices automatically fall back to Mode-0 (transparent) if the peer does not support compression. Mode-2 is full PPP with the complete Link Control Protocol state machine, allowing negotiation of compression parameters.

Mode-2 devices must support Mode-1 operation and fall back to it when connected to a Mode-1 device. This allows Mode-1 and Mode-2 devices to interoperate while giving advanced devices flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Old modems work in transparent mode with no squishing (Mode-0). Simple new modems use one fixed squishing recipe (Mode-1). Smart modems can talk about which recipe to use (Mode-2).

sections.title: DCE-Identifier and Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new LCP Configuration Option called the DCE-Identifier (type 25). This 3-byte option has a single Mode field indicating whether the device supports Mode-1 (value 1) or Mode-2 (value 2). Its presence tells the other end that the sender is DCE equipment that wants to establish data compression.

The minimum PPP feature set for DCE compression includes support for the LZS-DCP compression algorithm, Protocol-Field Compression, Address-and-Control-Field Compression, and the PPP Serial Data Transport Protocol. The RFC mandates LZS-DCP (based on Stacker-LZS) as the default compression algorithm due to favorable licensing terms, compression ratios, and efficient use of processor and memory resources.
sections.plainLanguage: DCE devices add a mode flag to say if they can do simple fixed squishing or smart negotiated squishing. They all use the same squishing method (LZS-DCP) so they understand each other.

sections.title: Mode-1 Operation
sections.content:
Mode-1 devices use a fixed set of LCP, LZS-DCP and SDTP configuration parameters with no negotiation. The required LCP Configuration Options are: Maximum-Receive-Unit of 1550 bytes, Address/Control-Field-Compression enabled, and Protocol-Field-Compression enabled. The Compression Control Protocol must support LZS-DCP (type 23).

For LZS-DCP compression, Mode-1 mandates Check-Mode 3 (sequence plus Last Coding Block), single history count, and Process-Mode 0 (None). The Serial Data Transport Protocol uses fixed parameters including Header-Last packet format, H-Only header type, and 10,000 byte maximum frame size. Mode-1 devices send only a predetermined set of PPP packets and revert to Mode-0 if configuration is rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: Mode-1 is like a recipe card: both sides use the exact same settings without asking. LZS-DCP does the squishing with one history buffer.

sections.title: Handshake and Mode Selection
sections.content:
When a Mode-1 device powers up, it sends an LCP Configure-Request containing only the DCE-Identifier option with Mode set to 1. If the peer responds with an LCP Configure-Ack, compression is enabled. If no response arrives within a configurable timeout, the device reverts to Mode-0 (transparent) operation.

A Mode-2 device first attempts full Mode-2 operation by sending an LCP Configure-Request with the DCE-Identifier set to 2. If it receives a Configure-Reject or a timeout, it falls back to Mode-1 by sending the Mode-1 configuration. A Mode-2 device can accept Mode-1 requests and respond with Mode-1 acknowledgments, allowing seamless downgrade when encountering a Mode-1 peer.
sections.plainLanguage: At startup, a modem says what mode it wants. If the other side agrees, it uses that mode. If not, it tries a simpler mode or gives up and sends uncompressed.
